author.description: My name is Patrik Bak, and I've lived and breathed the math olympiad for a long time. As a competitor I went to the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) three times and won bronze twice. Later, two of my own problems made it onto the IMO. I also enjoy lecturing and helping others prepare for competitions. Beyond math, I enjoy programming, and especially combining the two, which led to GeoGen, a tool for automatically generating geometry problems. MathComps is another outlet for both of those, and one that creates something nice and useful for the math community 😀
author.shortBio: Three-time International Mathematical Olympiad participant and two-time medalist; author of competition problems and the MathComps handouts.
author.title: About the author

next.registration: Since April 2026, MathComps has also been a registered nonprofit association in the Czech Republic, MathComps z.s., IČO 249 37 924.
next.text1: My long-term vision is more interactive tools. There's now Mathilda, an AI tutor who helps with solving the problems in the handouts, and who'll be in the competitions soon. I'm personally a big AI enthusiast and can see for myself how it helps me learn new things. Alongside that, I'd of course like to keep updating the archive and keep writing and adding to the materials and the competition guide.
next.text2: In an ideal world, I could see myself working on MathComps and related things like writing handouts full-time. This past year, that was ultimately made possible by a combination of a few income sources: the site itself was backed early on by <wincent>Wincent</wincent>, most of the site's handouts also grew out of <matika>Matika Česku</matika>'s math circles, and the newest addition is support from <gtf>Global Talent Fund</gtf>, which is sponsoring the upcoming competitions with AI feedback, starting 14 September 2026.
next.text3: If MathComps, or the thinking behind it, caught your interest and you'd like to help, financially or otherwise, or just want to talk, <link>get in touch</link>, every message makes my day ☺️
next.title: What's next

story.text1: For a while I kept telling myself it would be useful to have a searchable archive of Czech-Slovak problems, since I searched them often and digging through hundreds of PDF files isn't much fun. I also dreamed of how great it would be to search by keyword, quickly filter down to problems on sequences, and so on.
story.text2: It's much the same with handouts. I'm always writing some, for talks at events, and they stay unpublished, at best as PDF files that aren't the most practical: you can't easily hide hints or solutions and keep them close to the statements, or display them well on mobile.
story.text3: Beyond the personal angle, it always struck me that a single site where problems are easy to find and which also has handouts could be really useful for newcomers trying to figure out what the olympiad even is and what's out there. Some beginner-friendly materials would be welcome too, since I missed having a single place like this myself back when I was a student hunting down everything I could find about competitions.
story.text4: These motivations are what the current version of the site grew out of, and it offers an archive of problems, handouts, and a guide for beginners. There'll be more and more of this going forward, not just a bigger archive and more handouts, but new features too 😇

steps: Pick an open competition (how to choose a level is right below) 🎮
Start your clock whenever you like inside the entry window, usually two weeks ⏲️
From there you have a limited time to solve the problems 📋
You present your solutions to Mathilda and she gives you feedback 🤖
Your final marks come after the competition closes, from your conversations with Mathilda 🔢
Send a partial solution, or ask Mathilda for help if you cannot start at all: progress after a hint still earns marks 🙂

lines: No other AI, no outside help of any kind. These competitions train you to solve problems, not to have them solved for you.
The clock covers solving and writing to Mathilda both, and her replies are not always instant (we would rather she was accurate than fast).
Talk to Mathilda as long as you like, though the number of messages and the length of one message are limited, for reasons you can guess.
Marks come from the whole conversation, so there is nothing to gain from wringing a full solution out of her.
Please do not share the problems until the competition closes, so you do not spoil it for everybody else.
Do not try to hack Mathilda, to make her write you code or hand you a soup recipe. That gets you disqualified.

competitions.description: The most important competition is the Mathematical Olympiad (MO). However, there are plenty of other competitions and activities that are good as training for MO or even on their own 😇.

howToStart.description: At the beginning, there are always many options on how to start. Then there are many options on how to progress. The following advice aims to help with this process.

finalNote.text: The key is to enjoy the process. The world of competitions and seminars attracts many people, and it can change the life of each of them for the better 😊
finalNote.title: In conclusion

mathOlympiad.description: The Mathematical Olympiad is a competition in solving interesting problems, open to elementary and high schoolers alike, with an emphasis on justifying your reasoning. Each year it starts with a home round and builds up to the most prestigious international contest of all,

features: Week-long events with two days of math and the rest of the days full of trips and fun 🎉
The host country usually rotates, so you get to travel to many interesting places ✈️
A chance to meet people from all over the world who are just as into it 🤝

international.intro: The biggest draw is the international competitions.

mathOlympiad.sharedTasks: Czechia and Slovakia have shared problems but separate organizations:
mathOlympiad.tip: Don't be afraid to try solving higher categories, problems often don't require more complex knowledge and categories overlap. The best of the best often solved higher categories too.

otherCompetitions.description: Besides the olympiad and seminars, there are many other competitions, both team and individual, in all sorts of formats, mostly one-day, fun, laid-back events 😌

resources.description: A brief list of the most important study/community resources that are definitely worth knowing.

tips.ai: We all see that AI is getting better at math. It can be a quick helper when learning new things. Just be careful, as it's not always right and can make things up 🙃

seminars.description: Correspondence seminars are an integral part of Czech-Slovak mathematical culture.
features: Solving problems at home and sending solutions by mail (hence the name), although now mostly online ✉️
Several series of problems during the year 📝
Camps packed with fun and math as an essential part of them 🏕️
seminars.tip: Many people solve multiple seminars at the same time, both at elementary and high school level. It's also common for Slovaks to solve Czech seminars and vice versa. It's no coincidence that there's a big overlap between the best MO and seminar solvers 😉

whyCompetitions.description: Math competitions are not just about competition and math 🙂.
